comparator.name: Media, Kunst, Design en Architectuur
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted Dutch regulations and Study Guide establish 180 EC for the Dutch Media path. The first two years each have ten required 6 EC courses. Year three has 30 EC of open study, three 6 EC courses and a 12 EC individual thesis and colloquium. Entry to year two requires passing Academic English or Research Techniques. Entry to the second semester of year three requires passing year one and the year-two specialisation courses; thesis entry requires passing all courses in the first two years. The Dutch language test or refresher conditions the academic skills grade. Academic orientation and language testing carry no extra credits. The Media and Art routes have different research seminars and study trips. The regulations set the open-study approval and level requirements and allow a 12 EC internship with 18 EC of courses.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target cp-000106 is the generic Media, Art, Design and Architecture bachelor with no route/specialisation named in the registry. TER Article 10.2 confirms four formal, equally weighted specialisations available in the applicable academic year: Media, Art, Design and Architecture, one of which every student must choose at the end of year 1. Each specialisation contributes exactly the same 30 EC of year-2 specialisation-specific compulsory courses and the same 12-EC thesis/6-EC research-seminar structure in year 3, so none is formally larger, more advanced or more central within the curriculum than the others; the four fields are named together, in this order, in the programme's own title (Media, Kunst, Design en Architectuur) and are listed in the same order in TER Article 10.2. No official source (the curriculum overview, TER Article 10 objective/exit-qualifications text, or the specialisation descriptions) presents one specialisation as more representative of the programme's broad academic identity than the others; each is described only in terms of its own object of study. Because no route is clearly more representative and none is the least specialised (all four are equally specific, named specialisations rather than a generic/default option), the neutral tie-break in the route-selection rule applies: the official order in which the current curriculum names the specialisations is used, which selects Media, the first-listed specialisation. This selection was fixed before any UCR course was considered and does not depend on UCR fit. The registry target is Dutch; Article10.2 order, not the appendix annual-plan order, supplies this neutral tie-break. Language track and annual-plan basis are now explicit.

trace: Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles, techniques and cultural influences. Contribution: Partial relationship: UCR teaches Western painting and visual interpretation, while VU analyses images and objects across media, art, design and architecture.

Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools. Contribution: Quantitative business/social-science method companion, not humanities archival or visual analysis methods.

Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers. Contribution: Western philosophical context, not the VU intercultural philosophy syllabus.

This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world. Contribution: Partial historiographic relationship: UCR examines art history’s theories and disciplinary construction; VU explicitly integrates four fields.

Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies. Contribution: Partial exhibition relationship: UCR modern art, curatorial practices and museums intersect VU exhibition history/theory, whose wider design, architecture, festival and political mediation remain different.

Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts. Contribution: Partial contested-heritage relationship through African collections, colonial looting and repatriation. VU additionally teaches UNESCO World Heritage designations, policy, landscapes and critical management frameworks.

Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts. Contribution: Textual interpretation and research; not iconoclasm/image critique equivalence.

Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses. Contribution: Modernity and colonial/social theory context; not VU visual-culture public-event debates.

Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills. Contribution: Partial film/media-history relationship: UCR film form, cinema history and wider media introduction; VU traces visual mass-media production/distribution/exhibition and media historiography from the nineteenth century.
Examines printing, typewriters and other media technologies as material and cultural objects. Students study how these technologies affect cultural production and meaning.

Explores how media shape attitudes and provide answers through examples from TV and TikTok. Examines messages that teach fear, pity, admiration and allyship. Contribution: Partial media-analysis relationship: UCR American mainstream screens and storytelling/representation; VU teaches a broader formalism, ideology, participatory-culture and research-methodology framework.

Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project. Contribution: Actual environmental visual representation, not architectural/spatial mediation equivalence.

Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study. Contribution: Documentary analysis plus a very short documentary item; not VU current AI/infrastructure research seminar or professional production sequence.

Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.
Examines persuasion, framing and communication ethics. Applied projects connect persuasive techniques to sustainability communication.

Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work. Contribution: Poetry/performance/hybrid creative practice; singing/songwriting/music performance excluded. Not postmedium art theory equivalence.

Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to contemporary global cultures. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.
Studies painting, sculpture and architecture in Renaissance Italy through commercial, colonial and cross-cultural exchange.

Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern sustainability. Contribution: Ancient/global craft production and practical educational activity; not modern conservation training.

Explores the archaeology of community and democracy in early-democratic Greece, seeking ancient lessons on community decision-making. Contribution: Early Greek community/democracy archaeology; not modern urban planning.

In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century. 
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. Contribution: Athenian myth, politics, art/architecture and assembly simulation; not heritage management/conservation policy.

Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work. Contribution: General conflict/peacebuilding context; not heritage-specific UNESCO policy.

Develops a research question, evaluates primary and secondary historical sources, and culminates in a substantial research paper on the American Century. It is distinct from a museum exhibition catalogue or compulsory disciplinary thesis.

Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality. Contribution: Moral-reasoning companion; no heritage-conservation specialism.

Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties. Contribution: Human-rights legal/philosophical context; no heritage legislation syllabus claimed.

Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis. Contribution: Civil-society theory and empirical NGO/CEL enquiry; not art-history capstone or museum professional practice.

Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across ages. Contribution: Related cultural, historical, rhetorical or narrative perspective; not full VU specialist or professional equivalence.

alternatives.label: Media, Film & Communication
alternatives.labelReason: Media analysis, film adaptation and communication organize the option.
alternatives.concept: Study how film, television and other media tell stories and shape public life. Use film analysis, media history and adaptation to examine questions about race, the environment and changing technologies. Put those approaches into practice in a short documentary and other creative work.
progression: Every actual workbook prerequisite and assigned offering independently checked for all24placements; all courses7.5EC, four per semester, at least6advanced and PPD in Year1. Formal absence of prerequisites permits early advanced units; it is not a claim that they are introductory.

alternatives.label: Art History, Museums & Material Culture
alternatives.labelReason: Art history, museum study, and archaeological material culture organize the option.
alternatives.concept: Study how paintings, objects and collections acquire meaning. Follow Western and African art, Renaissance exchange and modern museums alongside archaeology and ancient material culture. Use art historiography and historical research to examine how objects and institutions shape interpretations of the past.
progression: Introductory art history precedes later specialist art and museum courses. Modern History and History of Empires precede the historical research seminar.
alternatives.distinctness: The art-history option adds archaeology, ancient heritage and historical research. It shares art historiography, museum study, Renaissance art and material media with the media option, whose main sequence is film and screen analysis.
traceOverrides: Studies printing and earlier media technologies as material objects, connecting their form and circulation to cultural production.

candidates.label: Art history and contemporary art
candidates.assessment: Eight art-history, museum and archaeology courses support an Art direction, including Renaissance art and early-modern exchange. The VU Art seminar adds specialist exhibition cataloguing and digital registration.

candidates.label: Design history and culture
candidates.assessment: Official Design direction and fashion/material-culture rows verified. UCR’s adjacent commercial product/marketing content does not supply sustained graphic design, fashion history and design theory.

candidates.label: Architecture, cities and spatial culture
candidates.assessment: Architecture direction verified but UCR has no sustained architecture/urban design/spatial-culture sequence. Adjacent planning alone cannot repair disciplinary substance; scheduling is secondary, not the reason to choose Media.

blocks: Foundations of visual, material & academic culture
Partial relationship: UCR teaches Western painting and visual interpretation, while VU analyses images and objects across media, art, design and architecture.

Approaching Visual and Material Culture is a broader first-week orientation to analysing the form, operation and functioning of images, objects and spaces across all four fields. UCR's closest course, Introduction to Western Art History, is already matched to the more specific Image and Object Analysis, and no other UCR course offers the same general cross-disciplinary orientation, so no counterpart is claimed.

Academic Skills Arts and Culture develops discipline-specific academic writing and presentation skills for arts-and-culture study. UCR's academic-skills training is distributed across every course's written and oral assessment rather than concentrated in one dedicated skills course, so no single counterpart is claimed.
Academic English MKDA is a language-of-instruction requirement for students entering an otherwise Dutch-taught track. UCR is already fully English-medium, so no disciplinary counterpart is claimed.
Historical development of visual & material culture

VU surveys the modern era across all four fields. UCR studies modern art and related history in separate courses.

History of Media, Art, Design and Architecture: Contemporary surveys the most recent period across all four fields. No further UCR course beyond those already matched offers a dedicated contemporary-period survey of media, art, design and architecture together, so no counterpart is claimed.
The Netherlands TM is a thematic module situating the programme within a specifically Dutch context. UCR offers no dedicated course on the Netherlands, so no counterpart is claimed.

selection.assessment: The media option has six media courses and Film & Text. The art-history option has eight courses in art, museums, archaeology and ancient heritage, supported by historical research. The options use different research objects and methods and differ by thirteen courses each. The art option includes Renaissance art and exchange without reproducing VU’s full early-modern survey, museum cataloguing seminar or conservation training. Product development and planning offer related applications but do not supply sustained design history or architecture and urban design.

notes.text: The UCR options cover parts of VU’s Media and Art directions. VU provides a broader foundation in design and architecture, specialist research seminars and a compulsory study trip and thesis. UCR offers related work in museums and material culture. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.

audience.programmeDescription: VU’s Media, Kunst, Design en Architectuur studies the history and theory of visual and material culture across four connected fields. A shared foundation leads to a Media, Art, Design or Architecture specialisation, open study, a research seminar and a thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options emphasize media and film or art history and material culture. VU combines all four fields in its foundation and provides specialist media and art research seminars. Both UCR options have less depth in design and architecture.

curriculum.limitation: The 180 EC plan includes a study trip, 30 EC of approved open study and a 12 EC thesis with colloquium. Dutch language testing, attendance and progression requirements apply.
